He also indicated that their attachment to them was of the utmost antiquity, such that there is no separating from it, with His words: ﴿was the end﴾, meaning the final outcome of ﴿those who were﴾, meaning the inhabitants of the earth, who were thoroughly engaged in its cultivation. Since the one who benefits from admonition needs only the slightest of it, He indicated this with the preposition, saying: ﴿before them﴾, meaning before their time, ﴿they were﴾.

Since the context concerns the disputation of Quraysh in order to refute the truth, while they heard the reports of the earlier peoples, it was as if they claimed to be the strongest of people. The situation therefore required emphasizing the report that the earlier peoples were stronger than them. He therefore affirmed the matter about which they were making claims, expressing this with the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl, the pronoun that separates the subject from the predicate and confirms it) in His words: ﴿they﴾, meaning the earlier ones, because of the outward and inward powers they possessed.

Since the basis of the dispute is strength, not number, and He said, as a resumptive statement (isti'naf) in answer to one who might ask, "What was their condition?": ﴿stronger than them﴾, meaning these (people). Ibn 'Amir read it as "minkum" (from you) with the kaf, as is in the codex of the people of Syria, by way of iltifat (the shift from third-person address to second-person address) to make the intended meaning explicit. ﴿in power﴾, meaning in essences and meanings, ﴿and in traces﴾ on the earth, the traces that were stronger, because some of their traces have not disappeared even to this day, though thousands of years have passed over them, whereas the later generations' traces are obliterated in less than a century.

Since their power and might were the cause of their self-admiration and arrogance toward the command of their Lord and their opposition to His messengers, and that was the cause of their destruction, He said: ﴿So Allah seized them﴾, meaning He, who possesses all the attributes of perfection, seized them with overpowering might, force, and dominance. Since nothing had been mentioned earlier to which their seizure could be attributed, He explained what they were seized for, saying: ﴿for their sins﴾, meaning those which caused their seizure. Nothing of that which had made them insolent, to the point that they transgressed against their Lord, availed them, and no intercessor interceded for them. ﴿And they had no﴾, meaning, of those partners of theirs who led them astray, like these and others, ﴿protector from Allah﴾, meaning from the One possessing all attributes of perfection, or from a being originating from His greatness and majesty. He emphasized the negation by adding the preposition, saying: ﴿from any guard﴾, meaning, nothing shields them from His will concerning them, neither from their partners nor from others. Thus it is known that those besides Him decide nothing.

It is also permissible that the first "min" (from) be an initial (ibtida'iyya) particle in its proper meaning, indicating that the seizure was of the utmost severity, because if it did not begin from Him (glory be to Him), there would be no protection for them, and it would not have remained for them. This is unlike one whom Allah punishes with a corrective punishment (ta'dib), for his punishment becomes the cause of his survival, because of the protection he gains from Him (glory be to Him).

(p-45) (p-46)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 40, verse 22:

When He (subhanahu) mentioned their seizing (akhdh), He mentioned its cause, the gist of which is that belittling the Messenger is belittling the One who sent him, in His saying: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the great seizing. Since the purpose of the surah is to classify people in the Hereafter into two categories, and they were one of the two main pillars of the discourse, He brought their pronoun and said: ﴿because it was that they﴾, i.e., those who were before, ﴿their messengers used to come to them﴾, i.e., little by little over past time, in a manner that Allah (subhanahu) decreed and executed, ﴿with clear proofs﴾ (p-47), i.e., signs indicating their truthfulness, with an indication so clear from the manifestness of the matter that no fair-minded person could deny it.

Since bare disbelief is sufficient for punishment, He expressed it in the past tense and said: ﴿but they disbelieved﴾, i.e., they caused disbelief, in place of faith, which their messengers' coming (peace be upon them) should have been the cause of, to result from their coming.

Since their disbelief caused them destruction, He said: ﴿So Allah seized them﴾, i.e., with the seizing of wrath, ﴿Allah﴾, i.e., the Supreme King. Since His saying ﴿but they disbelieved﴾ indicates the cause of their seizing, He did not say "for their disbelief" as He said earlier "for their sins," because the context guides to it. Since their audacity toward great matters is an act denying power, He said, emphasizing their action as the action of one who does not fear Him: ﴿Indeed He is Strong﴾, whom nothing overcomes, and He overcomes everything, ﴿Severe in punishment﴾.

And when that was a wonder, because the clear signs prevent one from disbelief, it became a supposition for one who denies the sending on this attribute, so the statement "We had indeed sent them thus" and Musa, peace be upon him, was among the most-sent with signs, He connected to that as consolation and warning to those who turned away, and as a pointer to those who gained insight, His saying: ﴿And certainly﴾. He turned the speech to the manifestation of greatness, as in the signs that He displayed in the presence of this (p-48) mighty king, of the terror and magnitude by which his self was made small, his resolve was belittled before it, and his perception was obliterated. So He said: ﴿We sent﴾, i.e., with what We have of greatness, ﴿Musa with Our signs﴾, i.e., those indicating Our majesty, ﴿and a authority﴾, i.e., a commanding matter, very great, against which they have no stratagem to resist any part of it, ﴿clear﴾, i.e., clear in itself, proclaiming to everyone who can be made aware of it that it is very manifest. And that matter is what used to prevent Pharaoh from reaching his harm, despite the power and authority he possessed.

﴿To Pharaoh﴾, that is, the king of Egypt. Since the notables are the first to whom a command is directed, for by their submission the others submit, he said: ﴿and Haman﴾, that is, his minister. Since it is among the most astonishing things that one would deny the Messenger when he has come to support him and rescue him from his hardship, he said: ﴿and Qarun﴾, that is, a relative of Musa, peace be upon him. ﴿They said﴾, that is, these and those who followed them. As for all others apart from Qarun, [their saying was that] at the beginning and at the end, by potential and by act. As for Qarun, his act at the end made clear that he was stamped with disbelief, even though he had believed at first. This was also his saying, even if he did not say it in act in that time, for he said it in the wandering (al-tih), which shows that he (p-49) never ceased to hold it, since he did not repent of it. ﴿A sorcerer﴾, because they were unable to overpower him. They did not say "a great sorcerer" (sahhar), lest anyone suppose that they were praising him for excellence in the science of magic, so that aspirations would be stirred to turn toward him to benefit from him. It is the predicate of an omitted subject. Then they described him with their saying: ﴿a liar﴾, out of fear that people would believe him. So He sent the most favoured of His servants to him, to the basest of His servants in His sight, to establish the proof against him. He granted him respite when he met them with denial, and bore with him patiently until He had made the excuse with him to the utmost extent.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 40, verse 25:

When He had summarized His matter entirely in these two verses, He began to detail it, saying, pointing to their hasty rush into obstinacy without any pause at all, which the omission of the subject and the restriction to the predicate, which is the locus of the benefit, indicate: ﴿So when he brought them the truth﴾ — that is, Musa, peace be upon him — ﴿from Us﴾ — that is, the matter established, which no one has the power to change any part of, being ﴿from Us﴾, by the dominion We possess — so a group of his people believed with him. ﴿They said﴾ — that is, Pharaoh and his followers — ﴿Kill﴾ — that is, a true killing by taking away the soul — ﴿the sons of those who believed﴾ — that is, in him, so they were ﴿with him﴾ — (p-50) they singled them out for this and left others alone, perhaps they would deny him — ﴿and spare their women﴾ — that is, seek to keep them alive by not killing them.

Since this was, customarily, a matter that turns a believer away from faith and turns back those who had believed toward disbelief, He indicated that He, glorified is He, broke the custom by nullifying it, so He said: ﴿And the plot of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾ — that is, they are estranged from the right path that leads to victory and success. For it did not benefit them at first in guarding against Musa, peace be upon him, nor in the end in turning away those who believed in him from their aim; rather it was in it that their ruin and destruction lay. Likewise are the deeds of the wicked toward the friends of Allah: none of them dug a pit of deceit for another of them except that Allah made him fall into it.

And Pharaoh said, when he had come to know his own incapacity to kill him and what he had seen from him had overwhelmed him with fear and terror, to the greatest of the disbelievers of that time, to the chieftains of his followers, (as he sought to ward off from himself what was being said, that he had not left Moses, peace be upon him, despite his contempt for him, except out of incapacity to deal with him, while giving the impression that his gods were the ones who repelled him from him and that, were it not for that, he would have killed him): ﴿Leave me, that I may kill Moses﴾, that is, leave me (p-51) in whatever state I am in. And he added to the deception of the fools and to his own exposure, in the eyes of the discerning, to disgrace by his saying: ﴿And let him call upon his Lord﴾, that is, the one whom he invokes and claims that He has favoured him by what appears at his hands of these marvels. Then he gave a reason for this in his saying, emphasized to inform that the matter is very grave, because among them were some who belittled his affair, saying that what he was in had no effect whatsoever, in order to draw near to Pharaoh and to show steadfastness in following him: ﴿Indeed, I fear﴾, that is, if you leave him, ﴿that he will change your religion﴾, that is, the one you are upon, of attributing events to nature, by what he calls to of worshipping his God.

When he had inflamed them with these words to join him against Moses, peace be upon him, he increased this with his saying: ﴿Or that he will cause to appear﴾, that is, through him (according to the reading of the majority, with a fatha on the letter of the present tense), ﴿in the land﴾, that is, all of it, ﴿corruption﴾. The two Madinan readers, the two Basran readers and Hafs read it with a damma, ascribing it to the pronoun of Moses, peace be upon him, and with the word corruption in the accusative, that is, by the corruption of livelihoods, for when he prevails over us, one mighty over those other than us, he will shed blood, take captive the offspring, and plunder wealth, so the world will be corrupted along with the corruption of religion. The accursed one called righteousness "corruption" because it opposed his corrupt way, as is the custom of every corrupter toward the reformers (p-52). Al-Kufiyyun and Ya'qub read "or that" meaning that he feared the occurrence of one of two matters: the change (of religion), or the manifestation of what he was upon, which he called corruption; and even if the change does not occur immediately, weakness will result from it.

Having informed them of the enemy's statement, He followed it with the announcement of the words of the one who was sincere to them, so He said: ﴿And Moses said﴾, refuting this statement and removing its effects, emphasizing what had become settled in souls concerning the power of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, I have sought refuge﴾, i.e., I have taken refuge at the outset of the message, ﴿in my Lord﴾. He encouraged them to take refuge in Him and strengthened them by His saying: ﴿and your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who is good to us all, so He sent me to rescue you from the enemies of the religion and the world, ﴿from every arrogant one﴾, i.e., every insolent, tyrannical one who magnifies himself against the truth, this and other than this, ﴿who does not believe﴾, i.e., there does not renew for him any affirmation, ﴿in the Day of Reckoning﴾ from his Lord concerning himself, while he knows that there must be a reckoning of him by the one who is under his hand from his subjects and slaves, so he judges his Lord by what he does not judge himself by. The meaning of seeking refuge is that none of them can reach my killing because of my seeking refuge. This is a matter that has been settled by the One who sent me for your deliverance, the One Who is capable of everything.

When the speech of the two chiefs had ended, and the custom of those who lack a divine order binding them is that their hearts scarcely gather together, and that some of them must openly declare what is in them, however great the standing of the king who governs them, and however hard he strives to unite his public and private factions, God the Exalted said, reporting the words of one of the followers on this matter: ﴿And a man said﴾, that is, a complete man in his manhood, ﴿a believer﴾, that is, firm in faith regarding what Moses, peace be upon him, had brought. Since a person, when tyranny has spread, may dwell among the people of hostility, and may give advice as far as he is able, this was conveyed by His saying: ﴿from the family of Pharaoh﴾, that is, from among their notables and leaders, ﴿who concealed his faith﴾, that is, who hid it with great concealment, out of fear for his own self. This is because a single person who breaks away from his tribe is exposed to a danger that does not threaten him when he is one of a divided group, and he kept it hidden in a way that would deter them from killing him without his declaring his faith outright.

When he saw that they had resolved upon killing him with a strong resolve, he gave it the name of killing, and said, denouncing it in the strongest terms: ﴿Will you kill a man﴾, that is, one who is great among men in body and in meaning. Then he gave the reason for their killing him in a way that contradicts it, saying: ﴿because he says﴾, that is, in order that he may say, even if only repeatedly: ﴿"My Lord"﴾, that is, the One who nurtures me and bestows His kindness upon me, ﴿"is Allah"﴾, that is, the One who unites the attributes of perfection, ﴿and he has come to you with clear proofs﴾, that is, manifest signs free of any ambiguity, ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the One from whom you have no kindness except that which comes from Him. And just as His lordship over him required that he acknowledge it, so His lordship over you should prompt you to acknowledge it.

Since his words were nearly an outright declaration of his faith, he joined to them what would cast doubt upon his cause and deter them from harming him. He said, indicating that his situation must be either that of a truthful or of a lying man, and placing first the oath, which is the more effective in removing accusation from him and the more likely to win acceptance from them: ﴿And if﴾, that is, while the situation is that if...

Since the circumstance was extremely constricting, as he stood among three great evils (their killing the best of people at that time, their bringing punishment, and their discovering his faith), the least that such a situation would drive them to is to accuse him, if some motive does not lead them to destroy him altogether. He was therefore motivated, by the need for brevity in admonition and haste to say the least possible, to drop the nūn, and so he said: ﴿"He is lying, then upon him"﴾, the Arabic here being ﴿يَكُ﴾ (yakun, "he be") with the nūn omitted, ﴿is his lie﴾, that is, exclusively: that harms him, and there is no harm to you from it. He did not say "or truthful," even though the circumstance demanded utmost brevity, lest he should give the intended side less than its due, thereby falling short in some measure of courtesy. He therefore said, displaying the verb of being (kāna) and turning away from what is in his own favour towards what is against them, balancing what he had mentioned against it and leaving it short of it, in order to show fairness and to repel accusation from himself: ﴿"And if he is truthful, some of what he threatens will strike you"﴾, that is, as a punishment from Allah, while his truthfulness benefits him and does not benefit you in any way, with the nūn of ﴿يَكُ﴾ again omitted for the same reason as before.

Since the wise person is one who looks after his own self and does not reject the words of his opponent without proof, and since the least that one should do to one who threatens someone whose signs of truthfulness have become evident is to take part of it seriously, he said, establishing the proof with part of it, without negating what lies beyond it, to show fairness and that he had not given the matter its full due, let alone partisanship for it, thereby negating accusation from himself: ﴿"some of what﴾ and he said ﴿"he promises you"﴾ rather than ﴿"threatens you"﴾, indicating that if they joined him, all that he had promised them of good would befall them, and if not, what he had threatened them with of evil would overtake them. The verse is an instance of ihtibak (a device in which something is left unstated on one side because it is indicated on the other): the mention of his being singled out for the harm of lying first is a sign of its opposite, namely his being singled out for the benefit of truthfulness second; and the mention of their being struck second is a sign of his being struck first. Its secret is that he mentioned the harmful in both places, because it is more effective in admonition, since the soul's nature is to hasten to flee from it. And there stood, in a situation greater than this one, as is reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ (the authentic collection) from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, may Allah be pleased with both of them: Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, and he was the manifestation of his faith, when the matter had grown grave with the actual beginning of the act, as the polytheists seized the collar of the Prophet ﷺ while he was circling the House. Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, embraced him while reciting this verse, and his tears were flowing down his beard, until Allah relieved him, by which time they had torn out much of the hair of his head, may Allah be pleased with him.

Since Pharaoh had accused Moses, peace and blessings be upon him, of desiring to spread corruption and of excess, after he had accused him of lying, this believer justified his words with a fine division, in which the two halves both apply to Pharaoh, to repel him, while the same division remains fit for Moses, peace and blessings be upon him, as Pharaoh had alleged about him. So he said: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One to whom belong the sum of greatness and the foundations of might, ﴿does not guide﴾, that is, to the committing of what benefits and the avoiding of what harms, ﴿one who is a transgressor﴾, that is, one who spreads corruption and oversteps the limit. It seems that he, may Allah be pleased with him, allowed that some of what he had been threatened with might be delayed, so that they would call it a lie; for this reason he said ﴿"some of what he promises you will strike you"﴾, and he tied the matter to exaggeration, saying ﴿"a liar"﴾, because the first step of one's abandonment and misguidance is to go deep into lying, whereas Allah guides one who is moderate and truthful. So if he is a liar as you claim, his lie will harm him, and he will not be guided to a way to free himself; and if he is truthful, punishment will strike you, and you will not be guided to what would save you, since you are characterized by both attributes.

When he had conjured up for them, through this speech, a meaning that could be given such an interpretation, he began to admonish them, displaying sincere advice to them and grief over them. So he said, reminding them of God's blessing upon them and warning them against losing it, and appealing to them by mentioning that he is one of them: ﴿O my people﴾. He used the form of direct address rather than the first person, to make his intent explicit, and said: ﴿The kingdom is yours﴾. He drew their attention to what they know of the turns of time by saying: ﴿today﴾. He alluded to the humiliation they had experienced at certain times by saying: ﴿dominant﴾, meaning prevailing over the Children of Israel and others. People of hardship always expect ease, and people of ease always expect hardship. He also drew attention to the One God, the Subduer, to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens, so that dominion over the earth follows by a fortiori reasoning. He expressed this with the particle of location, which indicates need, to frighten them, saying: ﴿in the land﴾, meaning the land of Egypt, which, because of its goodness and its gathering of benefits, is like the whole earth, over which you have overcome the people.

Since it is known from this that they do not possess the whole of existence, it follows that the true owner of all is the true God and the absolute King, whose command none can resist. Therefore no one among His servants should expose himself to what he has no power to withstand of His wrath. For this reason he said: ﴿Then who will help us﴾, meaning me and you. He included himself among them, to avoid mentioning harm directly after singling them out for the kingdom, to remove suspicion and to urge them to accept the advice: ﴿against the might of God﴾, meaning He to whom all dominion belongs. By using the particle of doubt, he indicated that His punishment of them is a possibility. The intelligent person accepts what is possible and strives to guard himself against it, so he said: ﴿if it comes upon us﴾, meaning in anger at this man who claims that God has sent him. It is also possible that he is truthful, indeed it is obligatory to believe so because of the proofs he has shown. In this statement there is a recording against them that they know God to be King of kings and Lord of lords. Likewise is the statement of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿You certainly know that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 102], and that Pharaoh's claim of divinity is nothing but pure obstinacy.

When Pharaoh heard what he could not refute, and was in a position where he feared the rest of his people if he were to behave outrageously regarding this believer, the listener became eager for his reply. God, exalted is He, informed that he responded with a response that was no response at all: ﴿Pharaoh said﴾, meaning to his people, as an answer to what this believer had said, indicating by his evasion from the substance of his reply that he was cut off, unable to refute any part of his speech: ﴿I show you only what I see﴾, meaning opinions. ﴿...only what I see﴾, meaning that it is the right course according to the extent of my knowledge; that is, what I have displayed to you is what I conceal within myself. Since the believer's speech contained an allusion regarding guidance, and since a person's heart and tongue may agree, and their agreement may be upon error, he said: ﴿And I guide you only﴾, meaning by what I have pointed to of killing Moses, peace be upon him, and other things, ﴿only to the path of right direction﴾, meaning that which I consider to be correct; I do not conceal one thing while displaying another. Perhaps in this there is an indication to them of what the believer's words were hinting at, for he had cast doubt upon his matter. This also shows that he was in extreme terror concerning the matter of Moses, peace be upon him, since he consulted his people about the matter and tolerated these repeated exchanges, from which it is evident that he was almost bursting with rage against him, yet he was restraining himself.

When it became clear to this believer, may Allah be pleased with him, that Pharaoh had been humbled by his words and could not confront him openly, he moved to a plainer style than the first. Allah, exalted is He, told us about him by saying, relying in his description on the past tense verb, because this was a context of admonition, which should be addressed to even the least of those characterized by faith. This came after He had mentioned his nobility in the description, because he was in a context of striving and defending the Messenger, upon him and upon our Prophet be the best of prayers and peace, a position that only one firmly rooted in the religion may undertake. ﴿And the one who believed said﴾, meaning after Pharaoh's words, which were colder than snow and which revealed his ignorance, his inability, and his humiliation. ﴿O my people﴾. He emphasized this because of what he saw among them of denial of his position and because he feared accusation from them. So he said: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you﴾, meaning from obstinacy regarding the matter of Musa, upon him be peace. Since the least that is feared is sufficient for the sensible person, and since Allah's power over all of them was on one level without any difference, their destruction would be like the destruction of a single soul. He therefore used the singular and said: ﴿like the day of the factions﴾, although the singular form is more awe-inspiring and more forceful in warning and more severe in pointing to the power of Allah, exalted is He, and that He is able to destroy them in the shortest time. (p-60)

When he had summarized, he then detailed and clarified, or changed after having terrified. So he began with those whose punishment was like their punishment and whose pattern was similar to their pattern: ﴿like the pattern of﴾, i.e. custom, ﴿the people of Noah﴾, i.e. in what overtook them of destruction, which annihilated them so that they could not withstand it, along with the strength they had in attempting and resisting what they wanted, ﴿and ʿAd and Thamud﴾, along with what has reached you of their tyranny. Since these were the strongest nations, he was content with them and summarized after them, so he said: ﴿and those who﴾. He indicated with the preposition the specificity of the punishment, lest it be said: this is the custom of time. So he said: ﴿after them﴾, i.e. close to their era, not all who came after them.

Since the implied meaning was: God destroyed them and did not wrong them, he expressed it generally, joined with what it contained of the report, with its evidence. So he said: ﴿And God is not﴾, i.e. the One who encompasses the attributes of perfection. Since it was in the context of admonition to them, and His aim was to turn them back from their error in every state, he suspended the matter on will, because when will is removed, injustice is negated. He made it indefinite for generality, so he said: ﴿wishing injustice﴾, i.e. renewing from Him that at some time He suspends His will with some kind of injustice ﴿to the servants﴾, because no one ever thinks that He wrongs His servants who are under His subjugation and at the disposal of His will and command. Whenever they do not know His right and wish to transgress against one who knows His right, He will certainly punish them, and otherwise His withholding would be injustice ﴿to the oppressed﴾. (p-٦١)

When the sun of resurrection and the light of the gathering had risen from the horizons of this admonition, because it is not at all fitting that a king would leave his servants to oppress one another without judging between them, while we see that most of creation dies oppressed by its oppressor and broken by its ruler, he knew with certainty that the death which no one has been able to escape, and no one ever will, is only a driving toward the abode of exposure and the arena of recompense for the debt, as the custom of kings is when they appoint someone to bring to them those whom they command to be presented, so that they may be exposed to them, in order that the manifestation of might and justice, and the signs of generosity [and bounty], may appear. He said: ﴿O my people﴾. And since they were deniers of the resurrection, he emphasized, saying: ﴿Indeed I fear﴾, and he used the particle of elevation, for added intimidation, saying: ﴿for you﴾. And since he had named it earlier, for what he mentioned, the Day of Meeting (al-talaq) and the Imminent (al-azifa), he here recognized that people in it are anxious and frightened, and that because of the multitude gathered, they call out and are called out to, for elevation or abasement, and other varied matters, whose totality indicates the manifestation of might and the humiliation of creation before what appears to them of greatness and majesty. So he said: ﴿the Day of Mutual Calling﴾, that is, its terrors and what occurs in it. The Mighty, glorified is He, calls out with His saying: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 60] and they call out: "Yes, our Lord." The angels call out with a voice that is heard from afar just as it is heard from near: "O so-and-so, son of so-and-so, come forward for the decision of the dispute." And it calls to the servant: "Indeed, hearing and obeying." The victorious is called: "Indeed, excellent is the reward of the doers." The loser is called: "Indeed, evil is the return of the wrongdoers." It is proclaimed concerning wretchedness and happiness: "Indeed, so-and-so has been made happy; indeed, so-and-so has been made wretched." The companions of the heights (al-A'raf) and the people of Paradise call out to the people of the Fire, and the people of the Fire call out to the people of Paradise. Everyone is called out to when death is slaughtered, and every people is summoned with its leader. The angels call to one another, having surrounded the two groups (humans and jinn) in ranks arranged in the order of the heavens in which they were, glorifying and sanctifying, and voices rise in clamor, some with joy and some with woe and destruction. The tongues of the fires call out: "Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?" and Paradise calls out: "Where are those who strive in the pleasure of God, and the patient?" So how wondrous a day it is, on which the disobedient and the obstinate are humbled, and those whose hearts were broken for God's sake are honored. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, and others, recited it with the doubling of the dal in al-tanad, as a verbal noun of tanad, from nadda al-ba'ir (the camel bolted) when it fled and scattered. This is like His saying: ﴿the day a man flees from his brother﴾ [Abasa: 34]. What was mentioned earlier concerning the omission and affirmation of the ya' in al-talaq is something the discerning can apply here.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 40, verse 33:

Since the custom of those who call out to one another is to come forward, that day is described by its opposite, because of the severity of its terrors. So He said, substituting or clarifying: (p-63) ﴿The day you turn back, fleeing﴾, meaning: [when] the tongues of the fire will burst forth and snatch up the people of disbelief, and will blaze with blazing sounds, so that the people of the place of standing fall prostrate [from fear of it. You will see every nation kneeling, and they will flee, and they will not head for any place except that they find the angels] lined up there, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And the angel will be upon its sides﴾ [al-Haqqah: 17]. And the caller will call: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, if you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass through except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman: 33].

Since the one who turns back in flight only intends, in his retreat, a stronghold that will protect him and hide him, or a group that will shield him and help him, He said, clarifying their state: ﴿You have no protector from Allah﴾, meaning: from the King, the Mighty, who has no equal. He went to the extreme in negation and said: ﴿from any defender﴾, meaning: any preventer who would keep you from what is intended. So you have no defender at all, for He, glory be to Him, grants protection and no one can be given protection against Him.

Since the implied meaning is: because of your misguidance in this world, your state on that day is acquired from your states in this day, He followed it with His words, generalizing: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray﴾, meaning: the King who encompasses everything, the Hidden within the robes of majesty, the Manifest in the manifestations of subjugation and beauty, [leaves him astray] with a misguidance He has imposed upon him. He is in the utmost clarity, by what the King has indicated: ﴿then he has no guide﴾, meaning: to anything that benefits him in any way. As for incidental misguidance, Allah removes it for whomever of His servants He wills, and this is not known except by the final outcome, as the Imam Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari said: whoever dies upon something, he is disposed to it.

(p-64) Since the sum of what preceded concerning their conduct regarding the affair of Moses, peace be upon him, is that he came to them with clear proofs and they doubted them, and since the passage ended with a warning against the punishment of this world and the Hereafter, it is followed by the doubt of their forefathers regarding the like of this. So He said, explaining that they deserve the punishment He warned of, so that they would give thanks for the blessing of Allah in granting them respite and would fear His vengeance if they persist in transgression. He emphasized it because of their denial that they had come with a proof. It opens with the particle of expectation (laqad), because their condition required the expectation of this and called for it: ﴿And certainly Joseph came to you﴾, i.e., your forefathers came to him, O people of the Copts, but He expressed it this way to indicate that they follow the way of their forefathers, as is the customary pattern of imitation, and that they are upon their natural dispositions, especially if they had not left their dwellings.

﴿Joseph﴾, i.e., the prophet of Allah, son of the prophet of Allah Ya'qub, son of the prophet of Allah Ishaq, son of the friend of Allah Ibrahim, upon them and upon our Prophet be the best of blessings and the most complete of peace.

Since his coming did not encompass the whole span of time that preceded Moses, peace be upon him, He introduced the preposition and said: ﴿from before﴾, i.e., before the time of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿with clear proofs﴾, i.e., manifest signs, especially concerning the Day of Mutual Calling.

﴿So you continued﴾ (with the vowel of the zay pronounced with a kasra), from zala yuzalu, i.e., you did not cease, while you yourselves were followers of your forefathers.

﴿in doubt﴾, i.e., encompassing you, and you did not reach the rank of conjecture ﴿about what he brought you﴾ of monotheism and what follows from it. And He indicated the persistence of their doubt by His saying: ﴿until when he perished﴾. It is as though He expressed it with "perished" to give them the impression that he was not held in esteem by them, and that he was only saying what conveys reverence for the sake of pure sincere counsel and consideration of the outcome.

﴿You said﴾, i.e., (p-65) from yourselves, without evidence, out of aversion to what he brought and impatience with him, in ignorance of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Allah will never send﴾, i.e., He who possesses the attributes of perfection.

Since their intention was the total negation, so that no sending of a messenger would occur at any time, however brief, He introduced the preposition and said: ﴿after him﴾, i.e., Joseph, peace be upon him, ﴿a messenger﴾. This is not an acknowledgment from them of his prophethood; rather, it is an addition by them to their doubt about his prophethood the denial of a messenger after him, and a restriction placed upon the Greatest King regarding His servants and His lands, and a report about Him that contradicts His perfection.

Since it was as though it were said: "This is a great misguidance; has anyone gone astray like it?", He answered with His saying: ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like this great misguidance of great affair ﴿Allah leaves astray﴾. He made the Name explicit and did not use a pronoun, lest the leading astray be restricted to the aforementioned aspect, and He made it the Majestic Name to magnify the matter, since the state is suitable for that. Likewise what follows it: ﴿Allah﴾, i.e., with what He has of attributes of irresistible power.

﴿whoever is a transgressor﴾, i.e., one who exalts himself over affairs, goes beyond the limits, and seeks to rise above the station of humans.

Since the context concerns doubt regarding the messenger and speaking by conjecture, which entails accusing the All-Powerful, glorified is He, of incapacity or of departing from wisdom, He said: ﴿a doubter﴾. (p-66) [i.e.,] he doubts what does not admit of doubt, and accuses others of what has no basis for accusation. That is, his habit is vacillation in religious matters, so that he hardly settles on any matter. There is no transgression or doubting greater than the state of the polytheist, for he withholds the truth from its people and gives it to one who does not deserve it in any way. This verse is evidence that the Copts, throughout the ages, as we observe, have no reliability in entering the true religion, nor steadfastness in righteous deeds.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 40, verse 35:

When it became clear beyond any doubt what Moses, peace be upon him, had brought of clear proofs (bayyinat), that their doubt about the prophethood of the one who had passed (Moses) and their certainty in judging the denial of the prophethood of the one who was to come (Jesus) was the greatest error, and that it is a kind of disputation (jidal) whose only purpose is to turn the one upon the truth away from the truth he holds to the error the disputant holds, He connected to that, by way of inference (istintaj), His saying, censuring them in an expression that covers others as well: ﴿Those who﴾, that is, a disputation from ﴿dispute﴾, that is, fight and contend with severe contention, ﴿concerning the signs of God﴾, that is, those encompassing the attributes of perfection, especially the signs that point to the Day of Mutual Calling (yawm al-tanad), for they are the clearest signs of His existence, of what He is characterized by in attributes and acts, and of what is permissible for Him or impossible for Him.

Since disputation conducted in the best manner (bi'llati hiya ahsan) is legislated, and this is what He commanded, [p. 67] He said: ﴿without any authority﴾, that is, without empowerment (taslit) or proof, ﴿that has come to them﴾, that is, from the One to whom all command belongs. ﴿It is greatly hateful﴾, that is, it is great, namely the disputation, which is implied before ﴿those who﴾. He explained what was left vague of this greatness by a specifier (tamyiz) transferred from the subject, so He said: ﴿hateful in the sight of God﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿and in the sight of those who believe﴾, that is, those who are His intimates.

Since the doer of this can only be one whose heart is darkened, the implied meaning is: "Those are the ones upon whose hearts God has set a seal." Then He connected to it, as a resumption (isti'naf), His saying: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like this great sealing, ﴿God seals﴾, that is, He stamps with a stamp that brings ruin, ﴿upon every heart﴾, [that is]: He to whom all greatness belongs. Since the act of every living being is only through its heart, He attributed the act to the heart in the reading of Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir in one of the two transmissions from him, with tanwin, and described it with His saying: ﴿arrogant﴾, that is, one who pretends to what is not his, and nothing of that belongs to anyone other than God,

﴿tyrannical﴾, that is, manifestly proud, strong, compelling. The reading of the rest is with the idafa (genitive construction), which is similar in that the sur is inside the heart, so that it encompasses all its individuals. However, the description with pride and tyranny applies to the person, not to the heart. It is clearer than the irregular reading (qira'a shadha) that places the heart before every, because [p. 68] placing every before a noun indicates the totality of the hearts of those who are characterized by this description. It is certain that the individual hearts are distributed among individual persons, since a person cannot have more than one heart. By contrast, when the heart is placed first, it may be claimed that the one person, and that the sur, is for the sake of gathering all kinds of pride and tyranny, so the meaning becomes: upon the heart of one person comprising every individual of arrogance and tyranny. And God is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 40, verse 36:

When he mentioned the aforementioned sealing (ṭab') of the heart, he indicated it by what he mentioned of the words and deeds of Pharaoh, coupling them (ʿaṭfan) to what had preceded of his own words and the words of the believer. For he intended what had no hope of attainment, out of vanity (tīh) and foolishness, arrogance and tyranny, because of the thickness of his heart and the corruption of his intellect, so that he became a laughingstock to everyone who heard of him. This is if he thought that he would reach what he desired. And if he intended by that to deceive his people, to repel them from following Musa (ʿalayhi al-salām) for a while, then he has proclaimed them to be ignorant, and to be extreme in lacking resolve, nobility and reason.

So the Exalted said: ﴿And Pharaoh said﴾, that is, after the words of this believer, turning away from answering him because he found no flaw in it: ﴿O Haman﴾, and he is his minister, ﴿build for me﴾, and he made him known by the intensity of his concern for it through the attribution to himself in his saying: ﴿a tower﴾, that is, a high building rising above it for everyone. Al-Baghawi said: it is not hidden from the observer, even if far away. Its root is from tasrīḥ (clarification), which is manifestation. His giving as the reason the hope (tarajjī), which occurs only in what is possible, is evidence that he was deceiving his people while he knew the truth, (p-69) for no sensible person would count what he sought among what is ordinarily possible. So he said: ﴿that I may reach the ways﴾, that is, the ways for which there are no other ways because of their greatness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 40, verse 37:

Since reaching them (the heavens) was an amazing matter, he (Haman) presented it in an arresting manner, to make the listener give it its due attention, magnifying its importance, so that the listener would long to learn its explanation. He said: ﴿the ways to the heavens﴾, i.e., the means that lead to them. Whatever brings you to something is a *sabab* (means) to it.

When he mentioned this means, he mentioned the result of it, saying: ﴿so that I may look up﴾ [al-Saffat: 55], i.e., perhaps this will bring about and result in my looking up ﴿to the God of Moses﴾. According to this reading, it is a conjunction (*'atf*) on ﴿I may reach﴾ [Ghafir: 36]. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read it in the subjunctive (*nasb*) as a response (*jawab*), to alert the reader that what the wicked man put forward is among the possible things, when in fact it is a wish for something impossible and not attainable in the usual course of things.

Since part of his purpose in this, while keeping his people from following Moses for a time, was to deceive them by saying: "I ascended and searched for what Moses said, but I found no validity in it," he first presented his statement, clarifying his state at that time, because he suspected that their hearts inclined toward believing Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿And indeed I think he (Moses) is a liar﴾. He left aside any discussion of whether Moses was lying about the message or about divinity. Since this was an amazing matter, namely that a person would claim that he could be imagined by minds to ascend to the sky, and that God, who is free of need of everything and who existed when nothing was with Him, would be in the sky or in some place among places (for every thing that is in something is in need of its place, and everything in need is incapable, and the incapable is not fit for divinity; if he had not come from God, he would not have been fit to be believed), the meaning would be: he did this (acted) in the manner of Pharaoh, because We had made it attractive to him. He added, for further amazement: ﴿And thus﴾, i.e., and like that great adornment, which dazzles minds. Since the one who causes harm is the act of adorning and not the specific one adorned, he put the verb in the passive, saying: ﴿was made attractive﴾, i.e., the one who adorns, whose command is effective, adorned it. This is truly God, Exalted, by His creating and by His imposing; for everything that enters existence among created things is His creation. The Devil is so called figuratively, by causing through whispering, which is also God's creation: ﴿to Pharaoh, the evil of his deeds﴾ in all his affairs. So he turned toward it, desiring it, despite being far from the intellect of the least intelligent of people, let alone those of high resolve among them, let alone kings. He obeyed it, and so did his people. ﴿And he was barred﴾ (by himself, and he prevented others, according to the reading with the *fatha*) and God barred him (according to the reading of the Kufans and Ya'qub with the *damma*) ﴿from the way﴾, i.e., the one for which there is in reality no other way, which leads to God, Exalted.

Since this context is such that the listener might suppose that Pharaoh had some kind of effective action, He negated that by saying: ﴿And the scheming of﴾ and He repeated the name rather than using a pronoun, lest it be restricted to one of the aspects of the matter, so He said: ﴿Pharaoh﴾, i.e., in nullifying the affair of Moses, peace be upon him, ﴿was only in ruin﴾, i.e., loss and great destruction encompassing him, from which he cannot escape. What he is given is only because he is carried along by it and subdued within it, as the situation revealed. This clearly indicates that if he had any independent action of his own, his act would not have produced loss.

When Pharaoh's claim was too plainly false to need explanation, the believer turned away from it explicitly, and alluded obliquely to what God related of him, that the destruction surrounded him, in his saying, addressing his people and seeking their sympathy three times. The first was in the manner of summary in the call, and the other two in the manner of detail. God the Exalted said about him: ﴿And the one who believed said﴾ [i.e.]: pointing to [Pharaoh's] statement, by turning away from it. He expressed it with the verb, indicating that it is fitting for the least of the people of faith not to belittle himself from admonition: ﴿O my people﴾, i.e., O you for whom I have no standing except through you, so I am not suspected in advising you. ﴿Follow me﴾, i.e., impose upon yourselves the following of me, because happiness is generally found in what a person dislikes. ﴿I will guide you to the path﴾ (p-72) of ﴿righteousness﴾, i.e., the way of guidance, because it, despite its ease and breadth, leads without fail to the goal. As for what Pharaoh said, claiming that it is the path of righteousness while it leads only to ruin, this is an allusion to him that is close to explicit statement.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 40, verse 39:

Since this was a supplication in general terms, and since all of the disease lies in turning towards the transient (al-fani), and all of the cure lies in advancing towards the everlasting (al-baqi), He said, as a resumption (istinaf) in answer to one who asked about the detail of this path, explaining that it is the turning away from what perishes to what endures, belittling the worldly life and diminishing its standing, because inclining towards it (al-ikhlad ilayha) is the root of all evil, and from it branches out whatever leads to the wrath of Allah: ﴿O my people﴾. He repeated this in order to increase their compassion, by way of their being his own people, so he is not suspected in his advice to them, for he wants for them only what he wants for himself. And since souls, being naturally disposed to illusion (al-wahm), do not reckon anything as existing except what is present, he emphasised, saying: ﴿Indeed, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment﴾. He belittled it by saying ﴿the worldly﴾, indicating its lowliness, and by saying ﴿a passing enjoyment (mata')﴾, indicating that it is a carcass (jifah), because in the language mata' is among the meanings of carrion; so one takes from it only as the one compelled takes from a carcass. This is because it is the abode of departure, of cessation, of provisioning and of moving on.

Since he opened with the dispraise of the worldly life, he followed it with the praise of the Hereafter, saying: ﴿And indeed the Hereafter﴾, because it is the goal in itself, ﴿is the abode of permanence (dar al-qarar)﴾, from which one does not move at all, (p-73) the enduring of everything of its reward and its punishment. So it is for enjoyment, benefit, luxury and expansiveness for whoever reaches it through good following, or for misery and destruction for whoever dares to violate the sacred prohibitions and treats their transgression lightly. Al-Asfahani said: One of the knowers (al-arifin) said: If the worldly life were gold that perishes and the Hereafter were clay that endures, the Hereafter would be better than the worldly life; so how much more so when the worldly life is perishing clay and the Hereafter is enduring gold, indeed more noble and more excellent.

Just as its bliss is everlasting, so too is its torment. Therefore encouragement toward the bliss of the Gardens and warning against the torment of the Fires are among the greatest aspects of encouragement and warning. The verse is an instance of ihtibak (interlocking ellipsis): mention of "enjoyment" first is an indication of the omitted "expansiveness" second, and "permanence" second is an indication of the omitted "moving on" first.

When al-Biqa'i had stirred people's resolve through this admonition to turn away from the abode of distress and sickness, and to turn toward the abode of majesty and beauty by serving the One of might and perfection, he answered, in reply to one who asked about how this is done, with what amounts to this: that it is by turning to good deeds and abandoning bad traits, connecting this through the manner of clarification to clarification, mentioning the outcome of each so as to deter one from what destroys and to encourage one toward what brings nearness, and indicating that the side of mercy is the dominant one. [Presenting first the evil they are upon, and warning them against it so that they may return:] ﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾, meaning whatever is bad, of whatever kind it may be: males and females (p-74), believers and disbelievers,

﴿then he will not be recompensed﴾, meaning by the King to whom there is no king but Him, ﴿except with the like of it﴾, as justice, without being increased upon it by the weight of an atom, nor made less than it. He enters the Fire if he has nothing that would expiate it. This is the Sovereign to whom it is fitting to turn in service, since He is the Judge, the Just, capable of requital and of equality in requital. The disbeliever, since he is resolved to persist in disbelief, his punishment is perpetual. The sinner, [since] he intends repentance, believing himself to be [in] disobedience and evil, his punishment is cut off. The verse is general in its scope, and whatever has been excluded from it by evidence is specified; thus all the chapter of crimes and other matters falls under it. As for one who says it refers to a particular matter, it follows for him that it is mujmal (unspecified), because that particular matter is not mentioned, and specification (takhsis) is preferable to generality (ijmal), as the people of legal theory (usul) have said.

When he had explained justice in punishment, he explained grace in reward, as an alert that mercy has preceded wrath. So he said: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾, meaning even if it is small. Since the kings they are accustomed to only employ the strong because of their need, he made clear that it is not so with Him, for He has no need at all. So he said: ﴿male or female﴾. Since deeds are not valid without faith, he stated its condition, saying: ﴿while he is a believer﴾, meaning a deed while the condition is that he is a believer. Since this is a context of encouragement toward His justice, His generosity and His grace, He made the reward a consequence of the deeds, and said: ﴿those (p-75) — meaning those of lofty resolve and standing — ﴿will enter the Garden﴾, [meaning] by the command of the One to whom all command belongs, after He has multiplied their deeds for them as grace. The verse is of the type of ihtibak (balanced omission): mentioning equivalence first as justice implies multiplication second as grace, and mentioning entry into the Garden second implies entry into the Fire first. Its secret is that He mentioned His grace in each of the two sides. ﴿They will be provided for therein﴾, meaning without any need for transfer at all, nor for means; and perhaps this is one of the secrets of using the passive form. ﴿Without reckoning﴾, because what is in it exceeds counting through its abundance. For the lowest of its people in rank, if all the people of the earth were added to him, it would suffice them without any diminution of his kingdom at all. This is of the category of grace, and God's grace has no limit, and His mercy has overcome His wrath. As for the recompense of an evil deed, it is of the category of justice, which is why reckoning occurs in it, lest injustice occur. Al-Asbahani said: So when we set the general threats against the general promises, the promise is preponderant because mercy precedes wrath, and thereby the foundations of the Mu'tazila are demolished.

And when he had reached the utmost in advising them, and concluded by informing them that people are of two kinds, the one who perishes and the one who is saved, and the outcome of their desire that he remain as they were would be destruction by the Fire, he said, rebuking them for the evil of their recompense, calling out to them, repeating the call to heighten the alert and the awakening from heedlessness, and reminding them that they are his people and his supporters, and conjoining it to his earlier call because it does not detail it nor fall under its ruling: ﴿And O my people, what is [the matter] with me that I call you to salvation﴾ — that is, what portion of benefits and interests [is there] for me — ﴿while you call me to the Fire﴾ and destruction through disbelief? Calling you to salvation with faith out of compassion for you, mercy toward you and acknowledgment of your right, while you have no such claim in calling me to the Fire.

So the verse is of the type of ihtibak (interweaving): the mention of salvation, which accompanies faith, is given first as an indication of the omission of destruction, which accompanies disbelief, given second; and the Fire, given second, is an indication of the omission of the Garden, given first. His aim is to shake them and stir their resolve toward shame before him, by reminding them that what they are doing to him is not among the traits of people of manliness, who repay his kindness to them with harm.

When he had informed them, in general terms, of how little fairness they showed, he explained it with his words: ﴿You invite me﴾, that is, you cause my call to fall upon your deities, ﴿to disbelieve﴾, that is, for the sake of my disbelieving ﴿in God﴾, that is, to conceal what must be made manifest, by means of the One who bestows upon me [everything]; for to Him belongs everything, and to Him belong the totality of dominion, might, greatness and majesty; ﴿and to associate﴾, that is, to commit association, ﴿with Him﴾, that is, to make for Him a partner. And since everything other than Him, glory be to Him, has nothing of its own essence except nonexistence, he indicated its insignificance by using the particle for non-rational things, saying: (p-77) ﴿of which I have no knowledge﴾, that is, no kind of knowledge of its fitness for any share of partnership. Thus, this is a call to falsehood concerning a matter which it is not permissible to undertake except by a decisive proof that admits no kind of association. And if there is no knowledge of it, it has no might and no forgiveness, and so it has no existence, because kingship is a necessary attribute of divinity and is the most evident of things; therefore, what is claimed for it is the most evident of things, yet it is in such a state that it is not known in any way whatsoever, so it is pure nonexistence.

When he had made clear that they were calling him to that which is nonexistent, let alone that it could have any benefit or harm at all, in a verbal sentence indicating the invalidity of their call and its lack of establishment, he explained to them that he was calling them only to that which possesses all perfection, and in whose hand alone lies benefit and harm. So he said, indicating by the nominal sentence the firmness and strength of his call: ﴿And I invite you﴾, that is, I now direct my call to you, and before it and after it.

﴿To the Mighty﴾, that is, the One who has perfect might, who overcomes everything and is not overcome by anything. And when he described Him with this attribute as a warning, the description of Him as a means of encouragement was rightly and decisively [apt] with His words: ﴿the Oft-Forgiving﴾, that is, the One for whom the erasure of sin, both in essence and in trace, is continually repeated, and none can do that except one who possesses the attribute of might. And whoever is rightly described by these two attributes is the One whom none of the attributes of perfection escapes his knowledge. So the verse is of the type of *ihtibak*: he first mentioned the absence of knowledge as evidence of knowledge second, and second he mentioned might and forgiveness as evidence of their omission first.

(p. 78) Since the lack of knowledge of a thing among the people of knowledge entails the lack of that thing in the fundamentals of the religion (*usul al-din*), what they were calling to was falsehood, and what they were calling him to was the truth. Therefore it produced with certainty His saying: ﴿Certainly﴾. Although it means "there is no doubt and no uncertainty at all," as passed in Surat Hud, where it carries the meaning of cause (*'illah*), [i.e.] "for that reason there is no doubt that" ﴿that﴾, i.e., that which ﴿you call me to﴾ from these rivals ﴿has no call﴾ in any respect, for it has no perception. This applies if what is meant is that which does not reason. If what is meant is something that reasons, it has no call that is acceptable in any respect, for no proof stands for it, nor even a misleading doubt, ﴿in this world﴾, which is the place of the apparent causes, because none of it has either of the two qualities. ﴿Nor in the Hereafter﴾, because what is not known to be divine is, in this way, such. ﴿And that﴾, i.e., there is no uncertainty that ﴿our return﴾, i.e., our great return by death, and the place and time of our return, is ending ﴿to Allah﴾, i.e., the One who encompasses the attributes of perfection in accordance with what His might requires, so He will recompense each person according to what he deserves. ﴿And that﴾, i.e., there is no doubt that ﴿the transgressors﴾, i.e., those who exceed the limits, the ones who are most deeply immersed in this attribute, ﴿they﴾, i.e., specifically, because of Allah's judgment upon them with this, ﴿are the companions of the Fire﴾, i.e., those who will abide therein and never leave it, as the meaning of companionship (*suhbah*) requires, because their excess necessitated the excess of their constant presence in the Fire, whose nature is excess. And it is known that its Lord does not repay an evil deed except with its like. (p. 79)

When he had established that there is no command except God's, and that the Return (*ma'ad*, the return to God) is unavoidable, the following was given as a consequence of this, in His saying: ﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾. That is, with certainty, by a promise that admits no failure, and it is near. (This is) when remembrance will not benefit you on the Day of the Great Gathering and the great crush, in which one foot is upon another, when you see the terrors, the punishments and the quaking, whether you accept my counsel or do not accept it. When he had mentioned their fear, from which nothing can protect them, he mentioned his own fear, in which he relies upon God to protect him from it. So he said, conjoining it to ﴿you will remember﴾ without the meaning of the *sin* (of future tense) being taken into account: ﴿And I entrust my affair﴾, that is: I now, because there is no summons except to God, (entrust) ﴿my affair﴾ in what you plot against me ﴿to God﴾, that is, the One who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, so He will protect me from you if He wills.

The author of *al-Manazil* (Sahib al-Manazil) said: *tafwid* (entrusting, delegation of one's affair to God) is subtler in allusion and broader than *tawakkul* (trust in God) after the occurrence of the cause. *Tafwid* is both before its occurrence and after it, and it is the very essence of *istislam* (submission). *Tawakkul* is a branch of it. It has three levels. The first is that you know that the servant before knowing (God) possesses no capacity, so he does not feel safe from (God's) scheming, does not despair of (His) help, and does not rely on intention. The second is witnessing compulsion (*idtirar*), so you see no action that saves, no sin that destroys, and no cause that carries. The third is witnessing that the Truth alone holds the dominion of motion and stillness, of grasping and extending, of separating and gathering.

When he tied his entrusting to the proper name that comprises and necessitates encompassing, he confirmed this as an explanation of his intention. Emphasizing it, because their conduct in their scheming against him is the conduct of one who thinks that He, glorified is He, does not see them [and does not help him], he said: ﴿Indeed God﴾ [and] repeated the Greatest Name as an explanation of his intention, (saying) that He is ﴿Seeing﴾, that is, of far-reaching sight ﴿of the servants﴾, outwardly and inwardly. So He knows who deserves help by his attributes of perfection, and He knows who schemes, and He turns his scheming back upon him by the encompassing (power) He possesses.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 40, verse 45:

When this counsel of his to them, and his seeking refuge with the King of kings, resulted in his being preserved from them despite the great peril, the Exalted said, informing that his assumption was correct: ﴿So Allah protected him﴾, i.e., He made for him a protection (wiqayah) that shielded him from them, by virtue of the majesty, greatness and perfection that belong to Him, the Glorified, as a reward for his entrusting his affair to Him.

﴿From the evil (sayyi'at) of what they plotted﴾, i.e., the severe calamities (shada'id) of what they schemed, both in religion and in worldly life. So He saved him along with Musa, peace be upon him, confirming His promise, the Glorified, by His saying: ﴿You and whoever follows you will be the victorious﴾ [al-Qasas: 35]. And since evil plotting (al-makr al-sayyi') only befalls its own people, He said: ﴿And there encompassed﴾, i.e., there descended, enveloping, after the encompassing by drowning (al-ighraq), ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾, i.e., all of them, Pharaoh and his followers, because of their persistence in disbelief and their scheming. The encompassing of Pharaoh himself is by way of a fortiori (min bab al-awla), even if we do not say that the term "al" (family/people) is shared between the individual and his followers, because the custom is that one does not reach all of a person's followers except after humiliating and seizing him; so this is an understanding by agreement (mafhum muwafaqah).

﴿A terrible torment (su' al-'adhab)﴾, i.e., the punishment that prevents anyone from enjoying it (mustaʿdhib). Then he explained that by His saying:

**The Fire**, meaning they are **exposed to it** (i.e., while they are in the barzakh, the intermediate realm between death and resurrection), **morning and evening**, meaning they go forth and return at the times when they take their rest and delight in food. This is their custom throughout the days of the barzakh. In this exposure there is an added distress beyond what has been transmitted in general, from what Malik, the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), and others narrated on the authority of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies, his seat is shown to him morning and evening. If he is one of the people of Paradise, then it is from the people of Paradise; and if he is one of the people of the Fire, then it is from the people of the Fire. It is said to him: 'This is your seat, until Allah resurrects you to it on the Day of Resurrection.'" Perhaps the added distress is that they are the ones being exposed: they are taken away in shackles, driven so that they may look at what Allah has prepared for them, whereas most people are limited in this to having their seats uncovered for them while they remain in their own places. (p-٨٢) In this there is added humiliation for them, like the ruler's presenting someone to the sword when he intends to kill him. This is their custom until the Hour arises. **And on the Day the Hour arises**, it will be said to them: **"Admit the people of Pharaoh"**, meaning: O people of Pharaoh, himself and his followers, because of their following him in what he misled them into, **"to the most severe punishment."** Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Hafs read it as an imperative verb (fi'l amr) from the causative form (al-ikhal). The sense is: We say to some of Our soldiers, "Admit his followers, because of their misguidance by him today, to the most severe punishment." If this applies to his followers because of their following him, then it applies to him with greater force, by way of a fortiori reasoning (min bab al-awla). This verse is a text regarding the punishment of the grave, as has been transmitted from 'Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 40, verse 47:

Since this account of Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, and Fir'awn (Pharaoh) is a matter exceedingly strange, few know it as it truly is, because it belongs to hidden knowledge. [Subhanahu] indicated this by His saying: ﴿And when﴾, that is: recount to them this which We have informed you of, from what happened in the earliest time, and it has no way to reach you except from Us, because they know with certainty that you never sat with any scholar. And recount to them what will happen in the time to come, when ﴿they argue﴾, that is, these whom We punish, ﴿in the Fire﴾, that is: their followers and their leaders dispute therein with what does not benefit them. ﴿Then the weak will say﴾, that is, the followers (p-83) ﴿to those who were arrogant﴾, that is, those who sought to be great.

Since, because of the severity of their condition, each of them disowns his companion, they emphasized their statement: ﴿Indeed, we were for you﴾, that is, rather than for others, ﴿followers﴾, that is, followers in submission, so you grew proud over people through us. According to the Basran grammarians, it (tabaʿ) is singular, like jamal (camel), and it may be plural, like khadam, the plural of khadim (servant). Perhaps he used it in this sense to indicate that they were in great obedience to them, as if they were one man's heart. Since the great one protects his follower, they made their question a consequence of this, and said: ﴿So will you﴾, that is, O great ones, ﴿bear﴾, that is, ward off, be sufficient, and bear on our behalf, ﴿a portion of the Fire?﴾

When he had brought the speech of the weak, in the present tense, as is the original form, and as an allusion, together with depicting the state, because it is more decisive regarding the length of their dispute and because it is more painful to them, the listener was eager to hear their reply. He then resumed the report about them in the past tense, to emphasise the certainty of its occurrence, as a rebuttal to what the weak might suppose: that the arrogant have the power of resistance and the pride of disdain. So He said: ﴿Those who were arrogant said﴾ [i.e.] from the severity of what they were in.

Since the followers had assumed that their leaders would avail them, they stressed their report to them with what contradicts that, and so they said: ﴿Indeed, we are all﴾, i.e., all of us are ﴿in it﴾, i.e., the Fire, each receiving from the punishment according to what he deserves, [equally] whether you argued with us or left off arguing with us, and your Lord does not wrong anyone. So even if we had power over anything, we would have relieved ourselves, and even if we asked that we be given more or less, we would not be answered, for this is the abode of justice, so leave us and what we are in.

Since the judgement of Allah, exalted is He, prevents what the criminal used to do in the world, namely ransoming [himself] and the binding of another to him, and since their request for relief was a request of one who may be such that his judgement is according to what judgements are, as among the judges of the people of the world, they gave a reason for their answer, stressing it, and so they said: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, i.e., the One encompassing the attributes of perfection, ﴿has judged between the servants﴾, i.e., with justice. So He admitted the people of Paradise to their abode, and the people of the Fire to their fire, and so no one avails anyone anything.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 40, verse 49:

When [the Qur'an] indicated that no one can avail another anything at all, it informed that when they saw that they were far from God, and that they were not fit to call upon Him, glorified is He, they hung their hopes on the intercession of the angels. So it told of this on their part by His saying: ﴿And those who are in the Fire will say﴾, that is, all of them, the followers and the followed, ﴿to the keepers of Hell﴾. In place of the pronoun, He placed His saying: ﴿Hell﴾, to show that their request is directed to the people of the rank whose nature and the nature of its keepers is to frown upon its inhabitants. This indicates that, because of the evil of what they are in, they do not reason, so they do not place anything in its proper place, as they did in the world: (p-85) ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾, that is, the One who has been good to you by making you not feel pain from the Fire, ﴿that He may lighten for us a day﴾, that is, in its duration, ﴿of the punishment﴾, that is, some of it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 40, verse 50:

When they (the guards) were asked, they began their answer anew, as a sign of the listener's eagerness for it, informing them, through its context, of the cause that placed them in a state of rejection and abasement, unfit to be addressed. So Allah the Exalted said, reporting about them: ﴿They say﴾, that is, the guards. Since the implied meaning is: "Did there not come to you intellects that guide you to the true belief?", he followed it with their statement, as a binding proof against them, a rebuke and a reproach for having wasted the times of answered supplication: ﴿Did there not come﴾. Since the situation was perilous, the aim difficult and hard to achieve, and they needed brevity, they said [indicating, by mentioning the verb of existence together with the situation's demand for brevity, the nobility of the Messengers, peace be upon them, in giving counsel that saves from fears, through miracles, gentleness, kindness, long forbearance, clemency and patience, together with the nobility of lineage, purity of character, good manners, beauty of appearance and form, gentleness of companionship, and the greatness of their positions]: ﴿Were there not﴾, with the nun dropped, with the present tense depicting the state, ﴿coming to you﴾, in a continuous manner, one thing after another, ﴿your messengers﴾, that is, those who are from among you, so you are worthy of listening to them and turning toward them, because kind is more inclined to kind and a human is more receptive to one like himself, ﴿with clear proofs﴾, that is, proofs than which nothing is clearer. ﴿They said﴾, that is, the disbelievers: ﴿Yes﴾ [meaning]: they came to us thus. Then they began their answer anew, in response to the eagerness that arose toward it, with a meaning whose outcome (p-86) is their not answering. They based on their report of not answering the Messengers, the non-answering of their supplication. So Allah the Exalted said, reporting about them: ﴿They say﴾, that is, the guards: ﴿Then supplicate﴾, that is: you now call upon Allah, or the people of Allah among the human messengers, or the angels, or others, or do not supplicate, for it will not be heard for you.

Since their being commanded to supplicate was bound to make them suppose it might benefit them, they followed it with what would dishearten them, because that is more painful, more wounding, more severe for them and more dreadful, with their saying: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is not﴾ — this was the original order, but he used the descriptive phrase to attach the judgment to it, so he said: ﴿except in error﴾ — that is, in going astray on a path that does not lead to the destination, just as they were in the world; for this world is the field of the Hereafter, whoever sows something in this world reaps it in the Hereafter, and the Hereafter is the fruit of this world, which bears fruit only of the kind that was planted in this world.

[p. 87] When the sum of what has preceded of this narrative, which is sweeter than drink and more precious than pearls strung upon the necks of the full-breasted maidens of equal age, is this: He, glorified be He, granted victory to the messengers over their peoples when those peoples intended to seize them, but they could not reach them. Then Allah destroyed those peoples in this world, and in the Hereafter He punished them with the severest punishment. Likewise, He granted victory to Musa, peace be upon him, and to the believer who defended him. The victory of the People of Allah in general is hidden, because they are tested and then the final outcome (al-'aqibah) belongs to them. Most dull-witted people, who are the majority of mankind, think that they have no victory. Allah the Exalted said, turning the speech toward the locus of majesty, because victory for them follows by way of inference (istintaj) from what has preceded, and emphasizing it as an alert to the foolish about what is hidden from them: ﴿Indeed﴾, meaning: by the majesty that belongs to Us, ﴿We shall surely help Our messengers﴾, meaning: against those who oppose them, ﴿and those who believe﴾, meaning: those who are marked by this description, even if they are at the lowest rank.

When life is pleasant and sweetened by victory and is clouded by its opposite, He mentioned it for this reason, and so that one would not imagine, were it omitted, that their victory would be of a base rank. So He said: ﴿in the life of this world﴾, by binding them to the path of guidance, which secures every success, and by proof and dominance. Even if they are overcome at certain times, the final outcome belongs to them, even if Allah were to appoint for their enemies someone who avenges them, though after a time. At the least, their enemies are not enabled to do all that they want with them. ﴿And on the Day when the witnesses stand﴾, meaning: in the Abode of the Hereafter, from among the angels, the prophets and the rest of those brought near (to Allah). It is the plural of shahid (witness), like sharif and ashraf, indicating that their testimony is eloquent in its domain because of their complete presence. This is what the masculine verb and the use of the plural of paucity (jam' qillah) point to, though the good ones are few, even though, relative to the people of the place of standing, they are like a white hair on the black hide of an ox. He expressed it this way to indicate the manifestation of the just judgment through attributes of sovereign might (jabarut) for the sake of equity (qist), so that He raises His friends in every respect and humiliates His enemies with every humiliation.

When He had described the Last Day with things that many people do not understand, He followed it with what made it clear in a manner that showed the utmost clarity regarding His support for them. So He said, as a substitution for what came before: ﴿The Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers﴾, those who were deeply immersed in putting things in other than their proper places. ﴿Their excuse﴾, that is, their making excuses, and its time and its place, by what is indicated by the fact that the verbal noun is of the mīmī form (ma'dhira), and even if it is great, and by what is indicated by the masculine reading of the verb. Thereby it is understood that they will find no defense except through excuse, and that it will not benefit them, because they make excuses only with lies: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], or with predestination: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 106]. ﴿And for them﴾, that is, specifically, ﴿the curse﴾, that is, distance from every good, along with humiliation in every harm. ﴿And for them﴾, that is, specifically, ﴿the evil abode﴾, which is the Fire that encompasses every evil. This is in addition to the difficult standing-places that precede it. And if this is theirs, then what do you think of what is upon them? It is known from this that for their enemies, who are the Messengers and their followers, there is honor and mercy, and for them there is acceptance of excuse and a good abode. Thereby the signs of victory became manifest, and what He had reported of the completeness of His power was confirmed.
